A designed ZrOCl₂/ethylene glycol deep eutectic solvent for efficient lignocellulose valorization

Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center of Efficient Processing and Utilization of Forest Resources, College of Chemical Engineering, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China
ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** Deep eutectic solvent Poplar sawdust Acidity regulation Enzymatic conversion

ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) hold great potential in biorefining because they can efficiently deconstruct the recalcitrant structure of lignocellulose. In particular, inorganic salts with Lewis acids have been proven to be effective at cleaving lignin–carbohydrate complexes. Herein, a Zr-based DES system composed of metal chloride hydrate (ZrOCl2·8H2O) and ethylene glycol (EG) was designed and used for poplar powder pretreatment. Zr4+-based salts provide sufficient acidity for lignocellulose depolymerization. The acidity of the DES was analysed by the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameter, and the results demonstrated that the acidity can be regulated by the DES composition. Under the optimum conditions (ZrOCl2·8H2O:EG molar ratio of 1:2), the DES pretreatment removes nearly 100% hemicellulose and 94.7% lignin. The recovered lignin exhibited a low polydispersity of 1.7. The cellulose residues deliver an efficiency of 94.4% upon enzymatic digestion. Moreover, the DES can be easily recovered with high yield and purity, and the recycled DES still maintains high delignification and enzymatic hydrolysis efficiencies. The proposed DES pretreatment technology is promising for biomass valorization.

# 1. Introduction Owing to the scarcity of resources and the depletion of energy reserves, biomass energy has garnered widespread attention [1,2]. Notably, lignocellulose has emerged as a remarkable substitute for fossil fuels owing to its abundant sources, high yield, and inherent renewability [3-5]. For example, poplar sawdust is a processing waste from the wood manufacturing industry and a rich resource for biorefining. However, the complex structure of lignocellulose, known as biomass obstinacy, poses a significant challenge to realizing its full potential for high-value applications [6-8]. Efficient pretreatment technologies are urgently needed to achieve more efficient degradation and utilization of lignocellulose components [9,10]. Currently, common pretreatment methods primarily involve the use of acids, alkalis, organic solvents, and other chemical solvents [11,12].

Among these lignocellulosic pretreatment routes, deep eutectic sol- vents (DESs) have attracted considerable attention due to their low cost, environmental friendliness and biocompatibility with enzymes [13,14]. Typically, DES is regarded as a eutectic mixture of two or more com- pounds containing a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) [10,15]. In general, the DESs used for biomass

pretreatment are mainly based on quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs and acids/alcohols as HBD, where the acidity of DES is closely related to the fractionation effect of lignocellulose [16,17]. To modulate the acidity of DESs, inorganic salts are introduced into the DES system as the third component. This addition facilitates the disruption of lignin- carbohydrate complexes (LCCs). For example, Xia et al. introduced the metal salt aluminum chloride (AlCl3) into the choline chloride (ChCl)/ glycerol system. The inclusion of this inorganic salt elegantly modulated both the coordination states and the acidity strength of the DES [11]. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the lignin fractionation ef- ficiency reached 95.5%, with a high purity of 94.4%. In another parallel effort, Wang et al. introduced ferric chloride (FeCl3) into a ChCl/glycerol system, resulting in significant fractional removal of lignin (78.9%). Moreover, the treated substrate exhibited a high retention of cellulose (95.2%) and remarkable enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (99.5%) [18]. Very recently, DESs with metal salts as HBA have become an ideal sol- vent for lignocellulose degradation [19]. In our previous work, we designed a DES with a Lewis acid (consisting of ZnCl2: lactic acid) and used it for lignin extraction from poplar sawdust. A DES with an opti- mized acidity resulted in 95.2% lignin recovery and improved the enzymatic efficiency of cellulose [20]. The incorporation of metal salts

has enabled DESs to show great potential in extracting lignin from biomass. Additionally, polyols like ethylene glycol are used as HBD in DESs because of their multiple free hydroxyl groups. These groups occupy hydrogen bonding sites in lignocellulose, weakening interactions between lignocellulose components and interactions with the hydroxyl groups of lignin. This interaction facilitates efficient lignin separation and enhances cellulose accessibility to cellulases [21].

Based on the above studies, this work designed a Zr-based DES sys-tem composed of ZrOCl2-8H2O and ethylene glycol (EG). Zr4+-based metal chloride provides sufficient Lewis acidity for lignocellulose pro-cessing [22], and the existence of EG is expected to tune the DES acidity and enhance the lignin isolation efficiency, thus facilitating the binding interaction between isolated cellulose and cellulase in subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis [23]. Poplar sawdust was selected as a substrate for pretreatment, and the pretreatment process is summarized in Scheme 1. The results showed that the ZrOCl2-EG DES could efficiently separate hemicellulose and lignin while retaining cellulose in the solid residue. By adjusting the pretreatment conditions, a high cellulose recovery ratio of 96.5% was achieved, with hemicellulose and lignin removal rates of 100% and 94.7%, respectively. Under the optimum conditions with a 1:2 M ratio of ZrOCl2-8H2O:EG, 110 °C and 3 h, the glucose yield ob-tained by enzymatic hydrolysis of the cellulose reached 94.4%. The enzymatic hydrolysis and chemical composition properties of the solid residue from each cycle were analysed to determine a sustainable bio-refinery strategy. The fundamental structural properties of the recycled DES were almost unchanged throughout the recycling cycles. More importantly, the pretreatment efficiency (delignification and enzymatic saccharification) was largely maintained after the recycling process. This study proposes a strategy for the design of metal salt-based DESS, thereby enhancing biorefinery efficiency.

## 2. Experimental section ### 2.1. Materials and chemical reagents Raw poplar sawdust was acquired from Xiyue Lumber Mill, Xuzhou, China. The poplar sawdust was pulverized into particles (ca. 40-80 mesh). The wooden particles were dried in an oven at 105 °C overnight before use. ZrOCl2·8H2O (99.0 %), LiCl (99.5 %), AlCl3 (97.0 %) and ethylene glycol (EG, 98.0 %) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Company. ZnCl2 (99.0 %) was purchased from Nanjing Chemical Reagent Company. Cellulase was purchased from Novozymes Investment Company. Milled wood lignin (MWL) was prepared according to a previously established method [11].

## 2.3. DES pretreatment and lignin recovery For DES pretreatment, poplar sawdust (1.0 g) was mixed with DES (20.0 g) and transferred to a glass flask (150 mL) for biomass pretreatment. Subsequently, the DES pretreatment was conducted at different temperatures (90, 100, 110, or 120 °C) for 1–4 h. After pretreatment, the mixture was separated by vacuum filtration while washing two times with a mixed solution of acetone and water (50 mL and 7:3, v/v). The solid component (residue) was collected and dried at 105 °C overnight and then stored in a desiccator. The liquid fraction was collected by rotary evaporation at 40 °C until a volume of approximately 35 mL was reached. Then, 300 mL of deionized water was added as a counter-solvent to precipitate the lignin. Lignin was recovered by vacuum filtration and then lyophilized by freeze-drying. The filtered liquid fraction was dewatered by spin evaporation to recycle the DES for the next cycle.

Morphological and microstructural changes in the pretreated substrates were determined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7600F) operated at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. All the samples were dried and sprayed with gold before testing. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra for the cellulose substrate and lignin were recorded using a Thermo Electron Nicolet-360 instrument. The determination of the degree of polymerization (DP) was based on the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 5351:2012, with the specific parameters described in the supporting information. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to determine the degree of crystallinity of the cellulose substrate (details in the supporting information). The viscosity of the DES was measured on a Brookfield digital Viscometer DV-II at a speed of 6.0 rpm. The effects of DES constituents (HBA/HBD molar ratios) on pre-treatment efficiency were investigated. Compared to the untreated samples, there is a significant improvement in lignin/hemicellulose removal rates with the addition of ZrOCl2:EG (Fig. 1c and d), and the pH of the DES solution decreases from 2.6 for 1:6 ZrOCl2:EG to 0.1 for 1:1 ZrOCl2:EG (Table 1). The ZrOCl2/EG system with a molar ratio of 1:6 presents a delignification efficiency of 56.7 %. This might be attributed to the restricted accessibility of Lewis acids (metal salts) to LCC linkages. By varying the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio from 1:6 to 1:4 and 1:2, the delignification efficiency increases from 56.7 % to 83.8 % and 94.7 %, respectively. When the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio changes from 1:2 to 1:1, the delignification efficiency is calculated to be 94.6 %. However, the cellulose retention rate decreases significantly from 96.5 % to 85.0 %. This indicates that the presence of EG molecules can protect cellulose from degradation. When the amount of added EG is too low, the cellu-lose chains are exposed to Zr4+/Cl- ions, leading to cellulose degrada-tion [23]. Table 1 shows that the K-T parameters of DESs are related to the HBA:HBD molar ratio. When the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio increases from 1:1 to 1:6, the α and π* values decrease from 2.43 to 2.09 and from 1.21 to 1.14, respectively. The hydroxyl groups of EG are abundant and

can interact with metal salts through hydrogen bonds. The amount of EG can optimize the acidity of DESs by regulating the hydrogen bonding density and strength, realizing the effective breakage of lignin- carbohydrate bonds and retaining most of the cellulose [23].

The effects of temperature on lignin and hemicellulose removal were determined and are displayed in Fig. 2a and b [28]. When the temper- ature changes from 90 to 110 °C, the delignification efficiency increases from 52.7% to 94.7%. A higher temperature accelerates the lignin removal process because of the improved DES activity and accessibility. Additionally, the DES mobility is enhanced at higher temperatures, facilitating the exposure of DES to LCC linkages and promoting lignin removal. When the temperature further increases from 110 to 120 °C, the cellulose retention rate decreases significantly from 96.5% to 82.6 %. This indicates that the cellulose is degraded under these relatively harsh conditions. Fig. 2c and d illustrate the effect of pretreatment time on lignin and hemicellulose removal. Extending the pretreatment duration allows DES to penetrate more thoroughly into the cellular structures of poplar, thereby enhancing the disintegration of lignin and the hydrolysis of hemicellulose. The efficiency of delignification notably increases, increasing from 61.3% to 94.7% as the treatment period increases from 1 to 3 h. Meanwhile, the removal of hemicellulose sub- stantially increases, reaching 93.2% to 100%, respectively. However, beyond 3 h, the delignification efficiency does not increase but rather decreases slightly, which may be due to the deposition of condensed lignin and humins on the solid cellulose surface [29]. ## 3.2. Cellulose substrate characterization Improving cellulose digestibility for glucose production is a fundamental goal in lignocellulosic biorefinery research [30]. The results showed that the glucose conversion of pristine poplar sawdust at 50 °C for 72 h is only 5.7% (Fig. 3a). After DES pretreatment at 90 and 100 °C, the enzymatic efficiency increases to 40.9% and 50.8%, respectively. When the pretreatment temperature increases to 110 °C, the glucose digestibility continues to increase to 94.4%. However, at a pretreatment temperature of 120 °C, the enzymatic efficiency decreases from 94.4% to 89.3%. It is possible that the pseudo-lignin formed during the pretreatment process is deposited on the cellulose surface and inhibits subsequent enzymatic digestion (Fig. S1) [11]. The performance of the optimal sample is 19.9 times greater than that of the untreated sample. This might be related to the high rate of lignin removal, which reduces the unproductive adsorption of lignin to the cellulase enzyme [21].

An in-depth examination of cellulose substrates was conducted to probe the impact of DESs on the efficiency of enzymatic digestion. The degree of polymerization of cellulose is another important characteristic that determines cellulase saccharification [31]. As shown in Fig. 3b, poplar sawdust has a DP of 1147, which is comparable to that of the majority of wood raw materials [21]. After DES pretreatment, the DP decreases significantly to 853 at 120 °C. A decrease in the DP indicates partial cleavage of the cellulose glycosidic bond, exposing more reducing ends and enhancing enzymatic saccharification [32].

FT-IR analysis (Fig. 3c) was conducted to investigate the chemical structure changes in poplar sawdust. The band at 1735 cm⁻¹ is attrib- uted to the stretching vibration of C=O in acetyl groups and carboxylic acids from hemicellulose (Fig. S2). After DES pretreatment, the peaks ascribed to C–O bonds in the spectra disappear, indicating the extrac- tion of the hemicellulose component. The vibrations associated with the β-glycosidic bond, C–O deformation, and C–H deformation appear at 898, 1030, and 1423 cm⁻¹, respectively [32]. Fig. 3d shows the crystal structure of the pretreated poplar samples. The crystallinity index (CrI), crystal size (L) and distance between atomic layers (D) of the pristine and pretreated substrates were deter- mined. As shown in Table 2, the CrI of the raw material is 44.8 %, while the CrI of the pretreated substrate increases to 56.4 % at 100 °C. This increasing trend indicates that amorphous hemicellulose and lignin are removed during pretreatment, which is consistent with the results of the component analysis. However, CrI decreases at temperatures of 110 and 120 °C, which is due to the decrystallization effect of the DES treatment [24].

The size of the hydrophobic lattice planes (200) in crystalline cel- lulose is considered crucial for cellulase adsorption [24]. According to the observations presented in Table 2, the D spacing (the interatomic distance between layers) of the cellulose remains relatively consistent. However, significant increases in the crystallite dimensions of the pre- treated cellulose are observed, especially at temperatures of 110 and 120 °C. The crystal sizes reach 3.14 and 3.15 nm, aligning with a discernible enhancement in the saccharification efficiency [35].

3.4. Cycle tests The recovery of DESs is critically important for assessing the eco- nomic viability of biomass refinement [38]. Fig. 6a illustrates the solid recovery and chemical composition of the cellulose substrate across 6 consecutive cycles. Each cycle shows an increase in solid yield and remarkable cellulose retention (>90 %). The recovery of the DES solu- tion at the end of each cycle was >95 %, suggesting its high recyclability (Fig. S4). The utilization of the ZrOCl2-EG DES in the process highlights its ability to achieve effective closed-loop recovery and reuse of solvents without imposing significant environmental burdens or costs. Fig. 6b illustrates a slight decrease in enzymatic hydrolysis performance following 6 cycles, probably due to the introduction of some impurities in the recycled DES (with an increased viscosity of 72.1 mPa·s and pH of 0.9 after 6 cycles of DES). On the basis of these results, Zr-based DES pretreatment has great potential for biorefineries and for the develop- ment of biofuels [39].

4. Conclusions This study describes a Zr-based DES system comprising ZrOCl2-8H2O and EG for poplar sawdust pretreatment. The Zr4+ ions in the salt provide Lewis acidity, which is essential for lignocellulose processing. The results indicate that DES pretreatment significantly eliminates hemicelluloses and lignin, thereby significantly reducing biomass recalcitrance. Under the optimum conditions with a 1:2 M ratio of ZrOCl2-8H2O:EG, 110 °C and 3 h, the glucose yield obtained by enzymatic hydrolysis reached 94.4 %, which was significantly greater by 19.9 times than that of the original biomass without DES pretreatment. The molecular weight of the DES-extracted lignin was 1501 g/mol, with a uniform distribution and a polydispersity of 1.7. More importantly, the pretreatment efficiency (delignification and enzymatic saccharification) was largely maintained after the recycling process. This study presented an emerging method for the effective fractionation and valorization of lignocellulosic biomass within biorefinery technology.

In particular, inorganic salts with Lewis acids have been proven to be effective at cleaving lignin–carbohydrate complexes. Herein, a Zr-based DES system composed of metal chloride hydrate (ZrOCl2·8H2O) and ethylene glycol (EG) was designed and used for poplar powder pretreatment. Zr4+-based salts provide sufficient acidity for lignocellulose depolymerization. The acidity of the DES was analysed by the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameter, and the results demonstrated that the acidity can be regulated by the DES composition. Under the optimum conditions (ZrOCl2·8H2O:EG molar ratio of 1:2), the DES pretreatment removes nearly 100% hemicellulose and 94.7% lignin. The recovered lignin exhibited a low polydispersity of 1.7. The cellulose residues deliver an efficiency of 94.4% upon enzymatic digestion. Moreover, the DES can be easily recovered with high yield and purity, and the recycled DES still maintains high delignification and enzymatic hydrolysis efficiencies. Introduction Owing to the scarcity of resources and the depletion of energy reserves, biomass energy has garnered widespread attention [1,2]. Notably, lignocellulose has emerged as a remarkable substitute for fossil fuels owing to its abundant sources, high yield, and inherent renewability [3-5]. For example, poplar sawdust is a processing waste from the wood manufacturing industry and a rich resource for biorefining. However, the complex structure of lignocellulose, known as biomass obstinacy, poses a significant challenge to realizing its full potential for high-value applications [6-8]. Efficient pretreatment technologies are urgently needed to achieve more efficient degradation and utilization of lignocellulose components [9,10]. Currently, common pretreatment methods primarily involve the use of acids, alkalis, organic solvents, and other chemical solvents [11,12]. Among these lignocellulosic pretreatment routes, deep eutectic sol- vents (DESs) have attracted considerable attention due to their low cost, environmental friendliness and biocompatibility with enzymes [13,14]. Typically, DES is regarded as a eutectic mixture of two or more com- pounds containing a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) [10,15]. In general, the DESs used for biomass pretreatment are mainly based on quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs and acids/alcohols as HBD, where the acidity of DES is closely related to the fractionation effect of lignocellulose [16,17]. To modulate the acidity of DESs, inorganic salts are introduced into the DES system as the third component. This addition facilitates the disruption of lignin- carbohydrate complexes (LCCs). For example, Xia et al. introduced the metal salt aluminum chloride (AlCl3) into the choline chloride (ChCl)/ glycerol system. The inclusion of this inorganic salt elegantly modulated both the coordination states and the acidity strength of the DES [11]. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the lignin fractionation ef- ficiency reached 95.5%, with a high purity of 94.4%. In another parallel effort, Wang et al. introduced ferric chloride (FeCl3) into a ChCl/glycerol system, resulting in significant fractional removal of lignin (78.9%). Moreover, the treated substrate exhibited a high retention of cellulose (95.2%) and remarkable enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (99.5%) [18]. Very recently, DESs with metal salts as HBA have become an ideal sol- vent for lignocellulose degradation [19]. In our previous work, we designed a DES with a Lewis acid (consisting of ZnCl2: lactic acid) and used it for lignin extraction from poplar sawdust. A DES with an opti- mized acidity resulted in 95.2% lignin recovery and improved the enzymatic efficiency of cellulose [20]. The incorporation of metal salts * Corresponding author. After pretreatment, the mixture was separated by vacuum filtration while washing two times with a mixed solution of acetone and water (50 mL and 7:3, v/v). The solid component (residue) was collected and dried at 105 °C overnight and then stored in a desiccator. The liquid fraction was collected by rotary evaporation at 40 °C until a volume of approximately 35 mL was reached. Then, 300 mL of deionized water was added as a counter-solvent to precipitate the lignin. Lignin was recovered by vacuum filtration and then lyophilized by freeze-drying. The filtered liquid fraction was dewatered by spin evaporation to recycle the DES for the next cycle. 2.4. Cycle tests The recovery of DESs is critically important for assessing the eco- nomic viability of biomass refinement [38]. Fig. 6a illustrates the solid recovery and chemical composition of the cellulose substrate across 6 consecutive cycles. Conclusions This study describes a Zr-based DES system comprising ZrOCl2-8H2O and EG for poplar sawdust pretreatment. The Zr4+ ions in the salt provide Lewis acidity, which is essential for lignocellulose processing. The results indicate that DES pretreatment significantly eliminates hemicelluloses and lignin, thereby significantly reducing biomass recalcitrance. Under the optimum conditions with a 1:2 M ratio of ZrOCl2-8H2O:EG, 110 °C and 3 h, the glucose yield obtained by enzymatic hydrolysis reached 94.4 %, which was significantly greater by 19.9 times than that of the original biomass without DES pretreatment. The molecular weight of the DES-extracted lignin was 1501 g/mol, with a uniform distribution and a polydispersity of 1.7. More importantly, the pretreatment efficiency (delignification and enzymatic saccharification) was largely maintained after the recycling process. This study presented an emerging method for the effective fractionation and valorization of lignocellulosic biomass within biorefinery technology. Introduction Owing to the scarcity of resources and the depletion of energy reserves, biomass energy has garnered widespread attention [1,2]. Notably, lignocellulose has emerged as a remarkable substitute for fossil fuels owing to its abundant sources, high yield, and inherent renewability [3-5]. For example, poplar sawdust is a processing waste from the wood manufacturing industry and a rich resource for biorefining. However, the complex structure of lignocellulose, known as biomass obstinacy, poses a significant challenge to realizing its full potential for high-value applications [6-8]. Efficient pretreatment technologies are urgently needed to achieve more efficient degradation and utilization of lignocellulose components [9,10]. Currently, common pretreatment methods primarily involve the use of acids, alkalis, organic solvents, and other chemical solvents [11,12]. Among these lignocellulosic pretreatment routes, deep eutectic sol- vents (DESs) have attracted considerable attention due to their low cost, environmental friendliness and biocompatibility with enzymes [13,14]. Typically, DES is regarded as a eutectic mixture of two or more com- pounds containing a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) [10,15]. In general, the DESs used for biomass pretreatment are mainly based on quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs and acids/alcohols as HBD, where the acidity of DES is closely related to the fractionation effect of lignocellulose [16,17]. To modulate the acidity of DESs, inorganic salts are introduced into the DES system as the third component. This addition facilitates the disruption of lignin- carbohydrate complexes (LCCs). For example, Xia et al. introduced the metal salt aluminum chloride (AlCl3) into the choline chloride (ChCl)/ glycerol system. The inclusion of this inorganic salt elegantly modulated both the coordination states and the acidity strength of the DES [11]. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the lignin fractionation ef- ficiency reached 95.5%, with a high purity of 94.4%. In another parallel effort, Wang et al. introduced ferric chloride (FeCl3) into a ChCl/glycerol system, resulting in significant fractional removal of lignin (78.9%). Moreover, the treated substrate exhibited a high retention of cellulose (95.2%) and remarkable enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (99.5%) [18]. Very recently, DESs with metal salts as HBA have become an ideal sol- vent for lignocellulose degradation [19]. In our previous work, we designed a DES with a Lewis acid (consisting of ZnCl2: lactic acid) and used it for lignin extraction from poplar sawdust. The ZrOCl2/EG system with a molar ratio of 1:6 presents a delignification efficiency of 56.7 %. This might be attributed to the restricted accessibility of Lewis acids (metal salts) to LCC linkages. By varying the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio from 1:6 to 1:4 and 1:2, the delignification efficiency increases from 56.7 % to 83.8 % and 94.7 %, respectively. When the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio changes from 1:2 to 1:1, the delignification efficiency is calculated to be 94.6 %. However, the cellulose retention rate decreases significantly from 96.5 % to 85.0 %. This indicates that the presence of EG molecules can protect cellulose from degradation. When the amount of added EG is too low, the cellu-lose chains are exposed to Zr4+/Cl- ions, leading to cellulose degrada-tion [23]. Table 1 shows that the K-T parameters of DESs are related to the HBA:HBD molar ratio. When the ZrOCl2/EG molar ratio increases from 1:1 to 1:6, the α and π* values decrease from 2.43 to 2.09 and from 1.21 to 1.14, respectively. The hydroxyl groups of EG are abundant and can interact with metal salts through hydrogen bonds. The amount of EG can optimize the acidity of DESs by regulating the hydrogen bonding density and strength, realizing the effective breakage of lignin- carbohydrate bonds and retaining most of the cellulose [23]. The effects of temperature on lignin and hemicellulose removal were determined and are displayed in Fig. 2a and b [28]. When the temper- ature changes from 90 to 110 °C, the delignification efficiency increases from 52.7% to 94.7%. A higher temperature accelerates the lignin removal process because of the improved DES activity and accessibility. Additionally, the DES mobility is enhanced at higher temperatures, facilitating the exposure of DES to LCC linkages and promoting lignin removal. When the temperature further increases from 110 to 120 °C, the cellulose retention rate decreases significantly from 96.5% to 82.6 %. This indicates that the cellulose is degraded under these relatively harsh conditions. Fig. 2c and d illustrate the effect of pretreatment time on lignin and hemicellulose removal. Extending the pretreatment duration allows DES to penetrate more thoroughly into the cellular structures of poplar, thereby enhancing the disintegration of lignin and the hydrolysis of hemicellulose. The efficiency of delignification notably increases, increasing from 61.3% to 94.7% as the treatment period increases from 1 to 3 h. Meanwhile, the removal of hemicellulose sub- stantially increases, reaching 93.2% to 100%, respectively. Cycle tests The recovery of DESs is critically important for assessing the eco- nomic viability of biomass refinement [38]. Fig. 6a illustrates the solid recovery and chemical composition of the cellulose substrate across 6 consecutive cycles. Each cycle shows an increase in solid yield and remarkable cellulose retention (>90 %). The recovery of the DES solu- tion at the end of each cycle was >95 %, suggesting its high recyclability (Fig. S4). The utilization of the ZrOCl2-EG DES in the process highlights its ability to achieve effective closed-loop recovery and reuse of solvents without imposing significant environmental burdens or costs. Fig. 6b illustrates a slight decrease in enzymatic hydrolysis performance following 6 cycles, probably due to the introduction of some impurities in the recycled DES (with an increased viscosity of 72.1 mPa·s and pH of 0.9 after 6 cycles of DES). On the basis of these results, Zr-based DES pretreatment has great potential for biorefineries and for the develop- ment of biofuels [39]. 4. Conclusions This study describes a Zr-based DES system comprising ZrOCl2-8H2O and EG for poplar sawdust pretreatment. The Zr4+ ions in the salt provide Lewis acidity, which is essential for lignocellulose processing. The results indicate that DES pretreatment significantly eliminates hemicelluloses and lignin, thereby significantly reducing biomass recalcitrance. Under the optimum conditions with a 1:2 M ratio of ZrOCl2-8H2O:EG, 110 °C and 3 h, the glucose yield obtained by enzymatic hydrolysis reached 94.4 %, which was significantly greater by 19.9 times than that of the original biomass without DES pretreatment. The molecular weight of the DES-extracted lignin was 1501 g/mol, with a uniform distribution and a polydispersity of 1.7. More importantly, the pretreatment efficiency (delignification and enzymatic saccharification) was largely maintained after the recycling process. This study presented an emerging method for the effective fractionation and valorization of lignocellulosic biomass within biorefinery technology.
